title: Why Teachers in England Need to Come to Terms With the Fact That the SoS for Education Will Perhaps Never Have Been a Teacher
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Writing shortly after Lucy Powell's appointment as Secretary of State for Education, Haili Hughes pushes back on the recurring teacher complaint that a new education secretary 'has never been a teacher.' She acknowledges why the grievance resonates, since teachers work in a field where everyone believes they understand the job and the profession is routinely caricatured, but argues that treating classroom experience as an essential qualification for the role is unrealistic. National system leadership and school-level teaching share some domain knowledge yet are fundamentally different jobs, and personal experience of what worked in one school or trust can mislead reform if mistaken for systemic evidence. She notes that no other ministry faces the same demand. Her alternative is that the Secretary of State should be surrounded by serving teachers and leaders from a wide range of contexts, especially the most challenging schools, and must have the judgement and humility to use that expert advice properly.
points: Hughes argues that expecting the Secretary of State to have taught is unrealistic because running the national system and running a classroom are different jobs with only partial domain overlap.
Lived teaching experience can bring credibility and illuminate policy, but she warns it can also lead a minister to mistake one school's success for a representative view of the whole system.

She observes the double standard that no one demands a transport secretary has driven a train, suggesting the criticism says more about teachers' sense of being misunderstood than about ministerial competence.
Her constructive demand is for a broad advisory bench of serving teachers and leaders, not London-centric and not cronies, drawn especially from the most challenging schools.
quotes: We work in a field where everyone thinks they understand what it is like to teach. Criticisms mostly centre around the bizarre idea that teachers are living the easy life - working from 9 until 3 with 12 weeks of holidays which they are paid handsomely for.

We wish that those making the decisions in the highest office understood the realities of what those at the chalk face experience on a daily basis. However, to have expected the Secretary of State to have served as a teacher for any length of time is unrealistic; as is treating teaching experience as an essential requirement of the role.

However, what has worked in one school or even in a trust is unlikely to work in every school in England. I can imagine it would be pretty easy to mess up here and design an unworkable reform or even mistake your own experience for a representative view of the whole system.

Weirdly, it seems like this sort of criticism only ever seems to be shouted from the rooftops with education. I cannot ever recall a time when I have heard people yelling that the transport secretary knows nothing as he has never driven a train.
Now, let me be clear, the SoS should be surrounded by serving teachers and leaders. These need to be from a wide range of schools and contexts - not just London-centric, not just pals.

However, perhaps the most important thing and one I hope Lucy Powell heeds, is that she also needs the judgement and humility to use this expert advice properly. Only then can we start building an education system our brilliant teachers can not only be proud of but can thrive in too.
